mcqs.question: A team builds an elaborate canary process to limit blast radius, but has no automated alerting and relies on customers reporting issues. What has this team actually achieved?
options: Full risk reduction, since blast radius is the only factor that matters
Limited real improvement — a small blast radius still causes damage for a long time if detection takes hours, since risk depends on all three factors together
No improvement at all, since detection time dominates the other two factors entirely
The same risk reduction as automated rollback triggers, since canaries and alerting are interchangeable
mcqs.explanation: Deploy risk is the product of blast radius, detection time, and rollback time — shrinking one factor while leaving another large still leaves meaningful risk, since a small blast radius sustained for hours before anyone notices still adds up to real damage. No single factor dominates entirely, and canaries and alerting address different factors, not interchangeable ones.

mcqs.question: What's the difference between a readiness probe and a liveness probe during a deploy?
options: Readiness gates whether traffic is routed to an instance right now; liveness detects whether a running instance is stuck and should be restarted
They are two names for the same check run at different intervals
Liveness gates traffic routing; readiness restarts unhealthy instances
Readiness only applies to database connections, liveness only to CPU usage
mcqs.explanation: Readiness answers "should traffic go here right now" — preventing a still-initializing instance from receiving requests it can't yet serve. Liveness answers "is this instance still functioning" — catching a deadlocked or wedged instance and triggering a restart. Their roles are the reverse of option three's claim, and neither is scoped to one specific resource type.

mcqs.question: Why is rolling back a database migration fundamentally harder than rolling back application code?
options: Database rollbacks require more disk space than application rollbacks
Migrations always take longer to execute than application deploys
Once new-schema data has been written, the old application code may not understand it — a plain artifact rollback doesn't undo data already written under the new shape
Databases don't support version control the way application code does
mcqs.explanation: The core issue is data, not tooling or storage: redeploying the old artifact reverts the code instantly, but any row already written under the new schema (e.g., a populated NOT NULL column) still exists and the old code was never built to handle it. Disk space, migration duration, and version-control support aren't the actual obstacle.

mcqs.question: What rule does the expand/contract migration pattern enforce at every point during rollout?
options: The old column must be deleted before any new code deploys
Both the old and new application versions must be able to run correctly against whichever schema state currently exists
The migration must complete within a single deploy window
New code must ignore the new column until the contract phase
mcqs.explanation: Expand/contract's entire purpose is ensuring app-code rollback never depends on rolling back the schema too — so at every stage, both app versions must tolerate the current schema. The old column is removed only in the later contract phase, migrations often deliberately span multiple deploys, and new code is meant to actively use the new column during the migrate step, not ignore it.

mcqs.question: A new release wrote data in a format the previous version can't parse, and a bug is found. Why might forward-fixing be safer than rolling back here?
options: Forward-fixing is always faster than rolling back
Rolling back would restore the old code, which may now mishandle the already-written new-format data — creating a worse data-consistency problem than the original bug
Rollback is technically impossible once any deploy has completed
Forward-fixing avoids the need for a code review
mcqs.explanation: Once incompatible data already exists, reintroducing the old code that can't handle it risks compounding the problem into a data-consistency incident, which can be worse than living with the original bug briefly longer while a proper fix ships. Forward-fixing is typically slower, not faster; rollback remains technically possible; and review requirements aren't what's at stake.

mcqs.question: A team's rollback runbook says "redeploy the previous version," but during a real incident they discover the previous artifact was already purged by the registry's retention policy. What does this reveal?
options: The rollback plan was never actually tested, so an untested assumption (artifact availability) failed exactly when it mattered most
The registry's retention policy is misconfigured and should never purge any artifact
This is expected and unavoidable — rollback runbooks can't account for registry retention
The team should have used a different deployment strategy entirely, like blue-green
mcqs.explanation: A documented rollback procedure that's never been rehearsed is only a hypothesis — this is precisely the kind of gap a periodic rollback drill would surface safely, in advance, instead of during a live incident. Registry retention policies are a legitimate tool when accounted for in the rollback design, and the fix isn't a different deployment strategy — it's testing the rollback path itself.
